query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of chromium to the NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility while maintaining its high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of chromium
generation.conditions: Room temperature and high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) conditions, as well as irradiation with helium ions
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution with chromium
generation.mechanism: The addition of chromium will reduce the lattice distortion and increase the ductility of the alloy, while the high entropy of the alloy will maintain its high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation tolerance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature ductility and maintained high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation tolerance
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1600 °C, irradiation fluence: up to 10^16 ions/cm^2
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of chromium to be added and the potential effects on the alloy's microstructure and properties

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of chromium does not improve the room-temperature ductility or maintains the high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation tolerance, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community. HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in that they have at least four principal elements, instead of one or two in the latter. It is a breakthrough to the alloy design in the traditional physical metallurgy, and it opens a new arena for explorations of new materials and new properties. Previous studies have indicated that HEAs have a high softening resistance at elevated temperatures, and sluggish diffusion kinetics. Therefore, HEAs are widely regarded as highly promising high-temperature materials. Before the high-temperature application of HEAs can be seriously pursued, a technical challenge in terms of the mechanical property needs to be tackled. Basically, single-phased HEAs have been found difficult to reach a reasonable balance between strength and (tensile) ductility. Single-phased fcc structured HEAs are ductile but not strong enough. Single-phased bcc structured HEAs, on the other hand, can be very strong but at the price of brittleness. To the best of our knowledge, there is no report of HEAs possessing an excellent balanced strength
